prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the case in which a specific, quantitative theoretical prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) was matched by nature seven years later (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018), and the result then proved reproducible across many laboratories and moire platforms. That is a discovery in the sense the prize criteria intend, not an accumulation of incremental refinements. Seven of eight members ranked it, three of us placed it first, and no one raised a scientific objection to the core observation. My materials perspective adds one point: this is a field that could have stalled on sample quality and twist-angle disorder, and it did not. The community learned to fabricate and characterise devices well enough that independent groups see the same phase diagram, and that robustness is what turns a striking observation into a settled discovery. The three credited names are also the only candidate on this shortlist where theory and experiment map onto a clean three-person split with unanimous agreement on who they are (all seven ranking members proposed exactly this trio).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the microscopic origin of the superconductivity, and much of the correlated phase diagram, is still unsettled, so a citation must rest on the platform and the observed states rather than on an explained mechanism. Eriksson and Danielsson are also right that three names cannot capture a community: Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, earlier twisted-graphene theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and other experimental groups (Dean, Young, Yacoby and others) are all outside the credited set. Device-to-device variation from strain and twist-angle inhomogeneity means some claims in the literature are sample-specific. If the committee thinks the field needs a few more years to separate robust physics from sample-dependent behaviour, B038 could be argued as slightly early, and that is the argument I take most seriously.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as a conceptually clean, independently confirmed precision-atomic-physics advance with a natural two-person credit, and argues recognition is timely given the discussion of redefining the second.
responses.response: I agree the Katori and Ye credit is the tidiest on the list, and the maturity is not in doubt; I ranked it fifth for that reason rather than out of doubt about the science. My reservation is about the prize criterion. A lattice clock is a superb measurement instrument, but the discovery content is the magic-wavelength idea plus a decade of systematics, and the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes already cover much of the enabling physics. I would also point out that a redefinition of the second has not happened, so the argument from timeliness rests on an event that has not occurred. I would keep B045 as a strong alternative, not as the lead, and I would be moved if colleagues can articulate what new physics, as opposed to new accuracy, the clock has revealed.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first, arguing it is an original, clearly delineated idea that defines the architecture of present superconducting processors, and rates twisted bilayer graphene only sixth because the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I take the circuit-QED case seriously; it was my second choice and the Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf trio is clean. I disagree on two points. First, on mechanism: the pairing question is the same kind of open issue that accompanied other prize-winning discoveries, where the observation was secure long before the explanation, and the prize rewards the discovery. Second, on timing, you yourself note that the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits, and Kroll, Mehlig and Lindroth all flag the same overlap. Awarding a second circuit-based prize immediately risks looking repetitive, and Girvin's absence from the credited names is a real attribution weakness that you also acknowledge. I would keep B026 as my first alternative if the committee wants a quantum-technology prize, but I would not put it ahead of B038 this year. I also note your disclosure that you work in this area, which seems appropriately candid.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first as the standard non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons, mature and validated, and ranks magic-angle graphene second, noting the pairing mechanism is unresolved and credit is spread across a large community.
responses.response: I agree with your caveats on B038 about credit breadth and about the unsettled pairing, and I have tried to build them into my case against. Where I differ is on DMFT as this year's prize. The framework is important and long overdue in some sense, but it is a theoretical method, only you and Mehlig ranked it, and you identify the problem yourself: Metzner, who introduced the infinite-dimension limit with Vollhardt, is not among the credited names, so a three-person prize would be unfair on the face of it. Mehlig also notes that the committee rarely rewards computational methods. I would be glad to hear whether you think the DFT+DMFT successes on real materials are sharp enough to count as a discovery rather than a technique; as of now, I see B037 as a longer-term candidate that needs a different attribution before it can compete.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube astrophysical neutrinos first as a genuinely novel instrument opening a new observational window, with a two-person credit of Halzen and Karle.
responses.response: The diffuse flux is a real discovery and the instrument is a remarkable achievement, so I do not dismiss it; I ranked it sixth. My difficulty is the same one you raise in your own uncertainties: IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds, and the decisive individual roles across AMANDA, construction and analysis are partly collective, so naming two people risks being arbitrary. The source identification, which is what turns a flux into astronomy, is still limited to a few objects. I would want the committee to decide whether the prize rests on the diffuse-flux detection or on the sources before settling on the citation. Of the candidates outside my preferred choice, I find it a less secure fit for the one-to-three-person limit than the circuit-QED or clock options.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle graphene first and topological insulators and quantum Hall effects (B023) second, stressing that B023 is a deep, general concept confirmed for well over a decade and, if anything, overdue.
responses.response: We agree on the lead, and I share your view that topological insulators are scientifically deep; I ranked B023 third. I am less comfortable with it as a prize configuration. You and Pearce both note that the credited set mixes theory, the HgTe quantum spin Hall observation and the quantum anomalous Hall realisation, and omits Mele, Bernevig, Zhang and Hasan, so the attribution is the real obstacle and the competing B040 entry shows that the committee cannot even agree on the packaging. The proximity to the 2016 topological-phases prize also weakens novelty. Being overdue is an argument for settling the attribution, not for choosing a contested trio now. If we decide it must be a topology year, I would want to resolve whether this is a single prize or a QSH part and a QAH part before voting.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene as a reason to wait, or accepts the discovery of the correlated and superconducting states as sufficient.
Whether the experimental credit should go to Jarillo-Herrero alone, given that Yuan Cao and other coauthors of the 2018 papers cannot be added under the three-person limit.
Whether a second circuit-based prize in two years (B026) would be judged distinct enough from the 2025 prize to be preferable to B045 as an alternative.
How to package the overlapping topological-insulator entries B023 and B040 and whether a topology prize is possible at all given the 2016 award.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration or the named alternatives: I have no documented connection to Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald, Bistritzer, or the circuit-QED and optical-clock candidates. My general connections (David Clarke at IBM, Chalmers and Japanese microscopy colleagues, the international microscopy federation) are not tied to any shortlisted person that I know of. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson ranks B026 first, but that is a point of disagreement on merit and not a conflict for me.
